findings.claim: The read-only instruction the engine prompt carries names run_command, Google's tool. Muse's write and shell tools have other names and are disabled by flags, so the prompt tells the model not to call a tool that does not exist while never naming the ones that do - the weakest link in the item 3 posture.
findings.trigger: Every muse run.

evidence.observation: One hardcoded line for all non-codex engines, justified in the comment by agy's F11/F12.

findings.verification: Run -Engine muse -DryRun and read the tools line of the assembled prompt.
findings.remedy: Move the tools line into the engine row and phrase it with Muse's own tool names and its disabled flags.

findings.claim: Item 10's case list omits precisely the paths this design changes: a denial-retry and a format-repair turn served by a muse fake (finding #3), the prompt-file argv (finding #2), the version-unknown harness (finding #10), a -Raw/prompt-only run, the -EngineExe path for muse (finding #4), and any case that pins the argv against the CLI's real flag spellings (--prompt-file, --output-schema, --reasoning-effort, --no-foreign-personal-context). The fake also has to reproduce MSP records with schema_version, a session stream and two terminal records, which no existing fake does for its engine.
findings.trigger: Reviewing the wave that adds muse on the strength of a green harness-engines run.

evidence.observation: The suite and the fake are agy-shaped (result events, conversation ids, agy wordings); nothing exercises the adapter indirection of the secondary turns.

findings.verification: Run RC5 to establish the agy baseline, then add the case list above and check that each new case fails before its fix.
findings.remedy: Extend item 10 with those cases, and make the fake emit a record set derived from a real sanitized probe so the record_type/payload paths are exercised verbatim.

findings.claim: No existing environment variable guard logic for non-codex engines. All engine processes inherit the full parent environment.
findings.trigger: Any API_KEY environment variable set in the bridge process will be passed to the muse child process, potentially triggering per-token billing.

evidence.observation: Start-Process is called without modifying EnvironmentVariables; no filtering or checking of environment variables exists for non-codex engines.

findings.verification: Run codex-consult -Engine agy with an API_KEY variable set and inspect the agy process environment.
findings.remedy: Add engine-specific environment variable filtering logic that checks for and either refuses or strips configured variables before launching the child process.

findings.claim: The tree check only monitors writes, not reads. It cannot prevent or detect file reads by the engine.
findings.trigger: Muse can read any file accessible to the user (including outside the repository, gitignored files, etc.) even with --disable-write and --disable-shell, and this will not be detected.

evidence.observation: The tree check compares before/after working tree fingerprints, but has no visibility into read operations. This is identical to the agy engine's behavior.

findings.verification: Run a muse prompt asking to read a file outside the repository; it will succeed and the tree check will not flag it.
findings.remedy: This is the established safety model for all external engines. To restrict reads, a scratch workspace with restricted filesystem access would be required.

findings.claim: No MSP record parser exists for muse. The existing Read-AgyEvents parser is specific to agy's stream-json format.
findings.trigger: Any muse run will fail to extract the reply, thread ID, or failure information.

evidence.observation: Only Read-AgyEvents and Get-AgyTurnOutcome exist for non-codex engine event parsing.

findings.verification: Attempt to run muse through the bridge; it will attempt to use the agy parser which will not recognize MSP records.
findings.remedy: Implement Read-MuseEvents and Get-MuseTurnOutcome adapter functions following the MSP format specification, equivalent to the agy implementations.
